chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Clef Club's performers, 3,500 members, and its closing by the legislature
summary: Local nightclub performers played better there after their jobs; with 3,500 members it ran almost three years before the Colorado legislature, under pressure, passed a law closing it.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Oh, the performers that would even perform at every nightclub all over the city (unintelligible) would come in after they finished their evening engagement. And they would get up and ask to perform. And they would perform before the other performers. And they would give a greater performance there at the after hour club than they did on the job they just finished.
Well, that's because you're playing for your peers, your colleagues, yeah.
You're playing for that particular audience and for your competitors

(Unintelligible), you know, because that was noticed by some of the nightclub operators that eventually came up there. The thing got so popular that they came up, wanted to know. What is this club? This Clef Club. What is all this? So they'd come up and they'd see some of their own performers, and they'd tell them, "You didn't sound that good at my place," you know, one of those things, you know, and oh --
How long was that in operation?
That was what -- about '67 to '70 or around that time?

Around '66, somewhere along there. And we had 3,500 members. They didn't all come up at once, thank goodness. But it was enough of them to keep us going, you know, regular. What I mean? And I had a job earlier that I played in a nightclub in Denver from 9:00 o'clock until 2:00, and then I had five minutes to get up there and go through 7:00 or 8:00 in the morning. This was seven nights a week. But it was a great thing, and we met a lot of beautiful people. And I tell you, we did so well up there -- well, financially and by being such a popular place -- the state legislature here drafted a law to close us. It was a terrible thing.

And -- but they had a little pressure from other sources, you know, here in Denver, Colorado. There isn't a day that passes that we go downtown where people say, "Do you ever think the Clef Club they could ever reopen? I've still got my card. We've missed that place." And it was a great place, man, because most of the members were the performers, and this was a place where they would get together and the only time they would have to see each other, you know, and talk -- talk music and get up and perform and one of those things, and actually it was an education, even for the younger ones, you know, that were eligible to come in.

And we weren't bothering anybody, weren't breaking any laws, and I just don't understand it. It was a real drag for us because we were known coast to coast on this thing, because when bands would come in town, they'd say, "Hey, where is this (unintelligible) Clef Club club that we've been hearing about, you know, so and so? Well, it doesn't start until 2:00 o'clock in the morning," you know. The guys said, "We'll be there," you know, and all the bands that would play these one nighters that would come in town. They would wait, man. They'd come up and they'd play.
